domain: Pre-modern luni-solar calendrical intercalation — the astronomer-priest's craft of holding a fast recurring count (the lunar month) in agreement with a slow count tied to an observed phenomenon (the solar/agricultural year), by inserting intercalary months on a dependable rule, carrying the epact, and re-anchoring against the re-observed phenomenon so the two counts never silently drift out of lock
axioms: Two cyclic counts of different length that are never reconciled DRIFT: run the fast lunar count as if it were the slow solar year and within a few cycles the month named for the harvest arrives while the fields are bare — internal consistency of each count does not prevent the two together coming un-locked.

A correction owed on the SLOW cadence must fire against the slow phenomenon, not the fast counter: insert the leap-month when the SEASON demands it (the solstice has slipped a full month from its named date), never merely because a fast cycle happened to end — firing at every fast tick over-corrects into chaos; firing at none lets the drift run a full season deep.

Intercalation must be BOUND TO A STANDING OFFICE firing on an observed rule, not left to whoever remembers: a leap-month declared at royal whim (or skipped in a distracted year) produces a calendar no one can plan against — the schedule is a law, not a courtesy.

A count RE-ANCHORED against a re-observed phenomenon each cycle self-corrects; a count COMPUTED once from a start-value and trusted forever accumulates every small error — an arithmetically almost-right rule (the Julian year, 11 minutes too long) drifts ten days over centuries because nothing re-checks it against the sky.

The EPACT — the standing count of how far the fast cycle currently leads or lags the slow one — must be carried and inspected, because it is the single number that says whether a correction is owed; a calendar that keeps no epact cannot even tell it has drifted.

Two authorities each keeping their own leap-schedule (two cities' calendars) diverge until a date in one cannot be honored in the other — concurrent cadences need a promulgated reconciliation rule with a common epoch, or every cross-reference silently mis-times.

A calendar reform (a redefinition of the count) is worthless unless PUBLICLY ANNOUNCED with an adoption point so every office adopts the new count on the same day — an unannounced reform leaves half the community dated on the old calendar.
primitives: the fast clock (the session/run cadence — a Stop hook, a /goal-met, a session close: ticks often)
the slow clock (the Goal cadence tied to its charter-condition actually being met: ticks rarely)
the non-even division (the doc's 'sessions close often while goals span many runs' — a fast cycle that does not divide evenly into a slow one)
the intercalary duty (successor-proposal / reflect+compound+verify / dormancy-notice — an act owed on the slow clock that must be inserted on a dependable schedule)
the intercalation office (the standing office bound to fire the correction on an observed rule — the Stop-hook goal-cadence tier or an obligation object, vs. whichever session happens to remember)
re-anchoring vs. computed drift (re-observing the durable Goal-entity/charter each terminal check vs. the /goal Haiku evaluator judging only surfaced session output — the Julian-drift hazard)
the epact (the standing lead/lag count the Goal entity must carry — sessions-since-a-run-advanced-it, runs-owed-vs-observed, turns-budget-consumed — that alone makes drift detectable)
over-correction vs. under-correction (a once-per-Goal duty fired per-session — leap-month every month — vs. owed at the true close but observed at no session)
the two-calendars fork (the strategized-collapse running old-chain and new-chain runs on different counts with no reconciliation rule)
the unannounced reform (a sylveste-lbkd/sylveste-3kol supersession decreed but never promulgated to the offices that schedule against the old count)
failure_mode: Reasons about cadence-alignment (which cycle triggers an act, whether two counts stay locked), not about concurrency mechanics — cannot judge whether two sessions race the same close, at-least-once semantics, or fencing; it sees a duty fired on the wrong clock where the saga lens sees a write-race, and may miss a genuine idempotency hazard.

Frames a dormant Goal as 'drifted out of calendar-lock, epact un-inspected', not as an ownerless office (waqf) nor a stranded liminal subject (rite) nor unconsolidated sediment — cannot judge succession-of-custodian, single-crossing validity, or settling residence-time; where those lenses see vacancy/strandedness/erosion, this lens only sees two counts un-locked.

Treats the strategized-collapse as two calendars needing a promulgated reconciliation rule, not as schema-versioning/in-flight-compatibility mechanics (kernel-migration) nor mechanical load transfer (joinery) — can flag a cadence-fork while missing whether the DefaultChain migration is technically safe or whether a seam is cut on the load-bearing member.

Does not evaluate whether the elicitation ritual elicited the RIGHT goal — treats the ritual only as what SETS the slow cadence's phenomenon (the charter condition the re-anchoring observes), so it can certify the clocks stay locked while missing that the condition itself is poorly elicited.

May over-apply the anti-drift terror to genuinely ephemeral C1 goals, insisting on a carried epact and a bound intercalation office where an intentionally throwaway session-goal correctly just ends — flagging a deliberate non-reconciliation as a drift defect.
